title: Vomiting and abdominal pain in a young woman with diabetes
summary: Work up an unwell 19-year-old in the emergency department, reach a diagnosis and start management.

review.notes: SYNTHETIC teaching case for the Phase 0 engine proof, loosely following UK JBDS (2023) adult DKA guidance, with ADA (2024) differences noted. Revised after an automated clinical-safety review on 2026-10-08. Thresholds must still be confirmed against the source documents by a clinician (PLAN.md §10, decision 10).

presentation.chief_complaint: Vomiting and abdominal pain for two days
presentation.vignette: A 19-year-old university student is brought in by her flatmate. She has been vomiting since yesterday, has central abdominal pain and looks unwell. She is breathing quickly.

history.label: When did this start?
history.response: Two days ago. The vomiting started yesterday morning.

history.label: Do you have any medical conditions?
history.response: I've had type 1 diabetes since I was eleven.

history.label: Have you been taking your insulin?
history.response: I stopped it yesterday. I couldn't eat, so I thought I shouldn't take it.

history.label: Are you thirsty or passing more urine?
history.response: I'm really thirsty, and I've been passing urine all the time.

history.label: Any fever, cough or urinary symptoms?
history.response: It's been burning when I pass urine for about three days.

history.label: When was your last period? Could you be pregnant?
history.response: My last period was two weeks ago. I don't think I'm pregnant.

history.label: Tell me about the vomiting.
history.response: Five or six times today. No blood. I can't keep water down.

history.label: Tell me about the abdominal pain.
history.response: It's all over the middle of my tummy, a dull ache. It started after the vomiting.

history.label: What medicines do you take?
history.response: Just my insulin: glargine 18 units at night, and aspart with meals.

history.label: Do you drink alcohol or use recreational drugs?
history.response: A few drinks at weekends. Nothing this week.

history.label: Any illnesses that run in the family?
history.response: My dad has high blood pressure.

examination.label: General inspection
examination.response: Unwell, flushed, alert but tired. Fruity smell on the breath.

examination.label: Hydration status
examination.response: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, reduced skin turgor.

examination.label: Respiratory examination
examination.response: Deep, sighing respirations (Kussmaul). Chest clear on auscultation.

examination.label: Abdominal examination
examination.response: Soft, mildly tender centrally, no guarding or rebound, bowel sounds present.

examination.label: Neurological assessment
examination.response: GCS 15, no focal neurological signs, pupils equal and reactive.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.response: Tachycardic, regular. Heart sounds normal. JVP not seen.

investigations.label: Venous blood gas
investigations.result: pH 7.12, HCO3 9 mmol/L, pCO2 3.1 kPa, K+ 5.4 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L

serial_results.result: pH 7.06, HCO3 7 mmol/L, pCO2 2.9 kPa, K+ 5.7 mmol/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L
pH 7.19, HCO3 11 mmol/L, pCO2 3.3 kPa, K+ 4.4 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L

investigations.label: Urea and electrolytes
investigations.result: Na 131, K 5.6, Cl 98, urea 9.8 mmol/L, creatinine 112 µmol/L

investigations.label: Full blood count
investigations.result: WCC 15.2 x10^9/L, Hb 145 g/L, platelets 310 x10^9/L

investigations.label: 12-lead ECG
investigations.result: Sinus tachycardia 118/min. Tall T waves in V2–V4. No arrhythmia.

investigations.label: CT head
investigations.reason: GCS 15 with no focal signs: no indication, and it delays treatment.

investigations.label: CT abdomen and pelvis
investigations.reason: Abdominal pain is common in DKA and usually settles with treatment; reassess before imaging.

treatments.label: IV crystalloid: 0.9% sodium chloride (or a balanced crystalloid)
treatments.response: 1 litre of crystalloid started over 1 hour.

treatments.label: Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/h)
treatments.response: Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion started at 0.1 units/kg/h (6 units/h for 60 kg).

treatments.label: Potassium replacement in IV fluids (guided by a potassium result)
treatments.response: 40 mmol/L potassium to be added to the fluids while K is 3.5–5.5 mmol/L, none while above 5.5; recheck K at 1 hour and 2-hourly.

treatments.label: Continue long-acting (basal) insulin
treatments.response: Usual glargine dose prescribed for tonight.

treatments.label: Antibiotics for urinary infection (local guideline)
treatments.response: Antibiotic prescribed per local urinary infection guideline.

treatments.label: IV sodium bicarbonate
treatments.reason: Not recommended in DKA at this pH; it can worsen hypokalaemia and cause paradoxical CNS acidosis.

treatments.label: Discharge with oral rehydration advice
treatments.reason: She has severe DKA and needs inpatient treatment.

treatments.label: Senior / critical-care review
treatments.response: Senior review requested; HDU team aware.

treatments.label: Hourly glucose and ketones, cardiac monitoring, strict fluid balance
treatments.response: Hourly capillary glucose and ketones, continuous cardiac monitoring and a fluid balance chart started.

treatments.label: 500 mL crystalloid bolus over 15 minutes
treatments.response: 500 mL crystalloid bolus given over 15 minutes.

treatments.label: Add 10% glucose infusion once glucose is below 14 mmol/L
treatments.response: 10% glucose to run alongside the fluids once glucose falls below 14 mmol/L.

treatments.label: Refer to the diabetes specialist team
IV insulin bolus
treatments.reason: JBDS advises against a bolus when a fixed-rate infusion is started (ADA allows an optional 0.1 units/kg bolus).

treatments.label: IV 5% glucose or 0.45% saline as the initial fluid
treatments.reason: Hypotonic or glucose-only fluid is unsafe as initial resuscitation in DKA; it worsens hyponatraemia and raises cerebral-oedema risk.

treatments.label: Variable-rate (sliding-scale) or subcutaneous insulin only
treatments.reason: DKA needs a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion; a variable-rate or subcutaneous-only regimen does not reliably clear ketones.

events.message: She is drowsier. Blood pressure has fallen to 82/48 mmHg and her heart rate is 132 /min.

ordering.label: Potassium result known before starting insulin
Potassium result known before replacing potassium

monitoring.label: Repeat venous gas to monitor response

debrief: This is diabetic ketoacidosis. JBDS (2023) criteria: glucose of 11 mmol/L or more OR known diabetes; blood ketones of 3 mmol/L or more (or urine ketones 2+); and pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L. ADA (2024) uses bicarbonate below 18 and would grade this moderate (pH 7.12) to severe (HCO3 9). Her heart rate above 100 and anion gap of 24 (Na − [Cl + HCO3]) are JBDS markers of severity, and a NEWS2 of about 7 means escalation: senior or critical-care review. Her potassium is high at the start despite a total-body potassium deficit: insulin drives potassium into cells, so check it before insulin, replace it once it is 5.5 or below, and recheck at 1 hour and 2-hourly. Young adults (18–25) are at higher risk of cerebral oedema: avoid over-rapid or hypotonic fluids and act on headache or a falling GCS. The trigger is a urinary infection, made worse by stopping insulin when she could not eat. The key sick-day rule is never to stop basal insulin.
model_pathway: Recognise the pattern: known type 1 diabetes, vomiting, polyuria, deep breathing; escalate early (NEWS2 about 7).
Bedside tests first: capillary glucose and ketones, then a venous gas for pH, bicarbonate and potassium; ECG for potassium effects.
Once a potassium result is back, start a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h (6 units/h for 60 kg); no bolus.
Replace potassium in the fluids once K is 5.5 or below; continue basal insulin.
Find the precipitant: urinary symptoms, dipstick and cultures; check for pregnancy; treat the infection.
Monitor: hourly glucose and ketones, repeat venous gas at 1 hour, fluid balance; add 10% glucose when glucose falls below 14.
Avoid bicarbonate, hypotonic fluids and unnecessary imaging.
